title: Router Network Activity

panels.title: WAN download
panels.description: Current receive rate on `wan` (internet → router), 1-minute average. CAKE shapes `lan` egress at 930 Mbit/s, so sustained values near that mean the shaper is the bottleneck.

panels.title: WAN upload
panels.description: Current transmit rate on `wan` (router → internet), 1-minute average. CAKE shapes `wan` egress at 900 Mbit/s.

panels.title: Conntrack table used
panels.description: Tracked connections as a share of `nf_conntrack_max` (262144). When it reaches 100% the kernel drops new connections. The `conntrack_table_filling` alert fires above 80%. Normal use here is well under 1%.

panels.title: CAKE drops/min
panels.description: Packets CAKE dropped per minute on `wan` (uploads) and `lan` (downloads to clients). Resolution follows the zoom: about 1-minute detail on short ranges, smoothed a little on 24h+. Bursts of drops during heavy transfers are the AQM doing its job; steady drops while the link is idle would mean the shaper bandwidth is set too low. See the CAKE row below for the larger view.

panels.title: Throughput (bits/s)
panels.description:
Traffic per interface. **Above zero = received, below zero = transmitted.**

- `wan` receive = internet download, `wan` transmit = upload.
- `lan` transmit = traffic to LAN clients (mostly downloads), `lan` receive = traffic from them.
- `wg0` = WireGuard tunnel traffic (already included in `wan` once encrypted).

Everything on one physical `lan` NIC: the four zones (green/kids/smarthome/guest) aren't split here.

Each point is the **peak 30-second rate** within that step, so short bursts such as a speed test show at their real height at any zoom (a 5-minute average showed a 930 Mbit/s test as ~270).

panels.title: Packets/s
panels.description:
Packet rate per interface. **Above zero = received, below zero = transmitted.**

Compare with throughput: a packet spike without a matching byte spike means many small packets (DNS floods, scans, VoIP/gaming) rather than downloads.

Each point is the **peak 30-second rate** within that step, so short bursts such as a speed test show at their real height at any zoom.

panels.title: NIC errors & drops
panels.description:
Errors and drops counted by the network driver/kernel at the interface, **before** CAKE. Should be flat at zero.

- `rx errs`: bad frames (CRC errors): suspect the cable, port or ONT/upstream router.
- `rx drop`: frames the kernel discarded on arrival. **A steady ~1/s or less on `wan` is normal noise**: the GFiber router and other upstream devices broadcast protocols this router doesn't use (STP, IEEE 1905.1 mesh, LLDP, vendor ethertype 0x9104) and the kernel counts each one as dropped. Only sudden spikes matter (then check `ethtool -S wan` for ring/fifo overruns). Running `tcpdump` on the interface temporarily hides them.
- `tx drop`/`tx errs`: rarely non-zero with CAKE in place; CAKE's own drops are in the panel below.

panels.title: CAKE drops/min
panels.description:
Packets CAKE deliberately dropped to keep latency low (AQM). Short bursts during big downloads or uploads are expected and healthy: that's CAKE preventing bufferbloat. Sustained drops with low throughput would mean the configured bandwidth is too low for the link.

CAKE only shapes **outgoing** traffic: on `wan` that's uploads, on `lan` it's downloads to clients. `wan` is set to 900 Mbit/s, `lan` to 930 Mbit/s (see `/usr/local/bin/router-shaping.sh`). Counters reset when the qdisc is re-created (reboot, `tc qdisc replace`).

panels.title: CAKE overlimits/s
panels.description:
How often a packet had to wait because sending it would exceed the shaper rate. This shows how hard CAKE is working, not a problem: high values just mean traffic was at the shaper limit (900 Mbit/s `wan`, 930 `lan`) and CAKE was pacing it. Near zero means the shaper isn't involved and the link itself sets the pace.

CAKE only shapes **outgoing** traffic: on `wan` that's uploads, on `lan` it's downloads to clients. `wan` is set to 900 Mbit/s, `lan` to 930 Mbit/s (see `/usr/local/bin/router-shaping.sh`). Counters reset when the qdisc is re-created (reboot, `tc qdisc replace`).

panels.title: CAKE queue backlog
panels.description:
Bytes waiting in CAKE's queue at scrape time (sampled once per scrape, so short bursts can be missed). CAKE targets about 5 ms of queueing; at 900-930 Mbit/s that is roughly 560-580 KB. A backlog that stays high means latency is building up on that interface.

CAKE only shapes **outgoing** traffic: on `wan` that's uploads, on `lan` it's downloads to clients. `wan` is set to 900 Mbit/s, `lan` to 930 Mbit/s (see `/usr/local/bin/router-shaping.sh`). Counters reset when the qdisc is re-created (reboot, `tc qdisc replace`).

panels.title: Tracked connections
panels.description:
Number of connections in the kernel conntrack table (NAT and the stateful firewall both depend on it), against the table limit (shown in the legend only, not drawn, so the entries line isn't flattened). If entries reach the limit, new connections are dropped and `dmesg` shows `nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet`.

A sudden jump usually means one device opening huge numbers of connections (torrent client, malware, scan). To find it: `sudo conntrack -L | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`.

Per-CPU drop/insert_failed stats aren't available: this kernel doesn't expose `/proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack` (use `sudo conntrack -S` instead).

description: wan/lan/wg0 traffic, NIC errors, CAKE shaping and conntrack. Hover the (i) icon on each panel for help.
